title: Balak: how goodly are thy tents (Numbers 24:5)
hookLine: the curse becomes a blessing, and his words now open the morning service

lines: THE FIRST WORDS AT THE DOOR.
cards: Walk into almost any synagogue on a weekday morning, and the first words many people say coming through the door are a line of Torah. It isn't from Moses, or David, or a prophet of Israel.
It was first spoken by a foreign seer, hired by an enemy king, standing on a hill and trying to curse the people below. Balaam's third try, at Peor.
He looks out over the camp of Israel, spread out tribe by tribe in the valley. And instead of a curse, these words come out.

teach.h: MAH TOVU: HOW GOODLY ARE THY TENTS.
teach.b: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, the first two words are Mah tovu: how good. What did he see that was so good?
The Talmud, and Rashi after it, give a surprising answer.

teach.h: DOORS THAT DIDN'T FACE EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Balaam saw that the entrances of their tents didn't face one another. Nobody could look straight into a neighbor's home. Living close together, they still gave each other privacy.
That's the goodness he saw: not grandeur, but decency between neighbors. The Talmud also gives Balaam's blessings a darker reading.
Rabbi Yochanan said, in paraphrase, from the blessings of that wicked man you can learn what curses he meant to say.
And the rabbis later read tents and dwellings as the houses of prayer and study, where Israel would gather. Then came the prayer book.

teach.h: THE OPENING OF THE MORNING SERVICE.
teach.b: Mah Tovu became the opening of the morning service, the verse said on entering the synagogue, followed by lines from the Psalms about coming into God's house. Not everyone was comfortable starting the day with Balaam.

A sixteenth-century rabbi, Solomon Luria, is reported to have begun from the second verse instead, because the first came from Balaam's mouth. Most prayer books kept it anyway. There's something fitting in that.

teach.h: A CURSE THAT BECAME A FIRST WORD.
teach.b: Words bought to curse, said by someone who'd rather not have said them, became the first thing many Jews say every morning. The blessing outlived the man and the money.

how: Many Jews say Mah Tovu on entering the synagogue in the morning; in most prayer books it opens the morning service, followed by verses from the Psalms about coming into God's house.

o: a song sung as the Torah goes back in the ark
a blessing said on leaving the synagogue
how good: the words that open the morning service

games.q: you're compiling a prayer book. the most beautiful verse for entering a synagogue was spoken by a hired enemy seer. do you use it?
o: leave it out: consider the source.
use it, but only on festivals.
games.why: most prayer books open the morning service with Mah Tovu. a blessing bought to be a curse became the first words many Jews say each morning.

practice: Picture the next room you'll walk into: your kitchen, your office, a classroom, a friend's home.

If you pray, you can say as you cross the threshold, how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, thy dwellings, O Israel; if you don't, simply pause in the doorway for one breath and look for one good thing about the place and the people in it.

wordCard.voice: Mah Tovu. How good. Balaam's blessing over Israel's tents, now the first words of the morning service.

carryVoice: Your line: how goodly are thy tents. The goodness was in doors that gave each other room. That's day four hundred sixty-four.
